records.sourceFile: Stability of salivary microRNA measures across an NCAA Division 1 football season - Implications for microRNA as a biomarker of concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Campbell TR, Zamponi M, Leathers D, Cavallario J, Martinez JC, Mollica PA. Stability of salivary microRNA measures across an NCAA Division I football season: Implications for microRNA as a biomarker of concussion. PLoS One. 2026;21(1):e0339614.
paper.abstract: This prospective study measured six pre-selected salivary microRNAs in 50 male NCAA Division I football players before and after one season. No microRNA changed significantly, but reliability across the season was low to moderate, so the markers may vary for reasons other than concussion.
paper.tldr: Six salivary microRNAs did not change on average over a football season, but most were unreliable between pre-season and post-season samples. The authors advise against using this panel for concussion decisions in its current form.
paper.methods: Prospective, observational study of 50 medically cleared male NCAA Division I football players. Saliva was collected before the first pre-season practice and within 72 hours of the final game, and quantitative PCR measured six target microRNAs with miR-361-5p as the endogenous control. Pre- and post-season values were compared with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and reliability was assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients.
paper.findings: Forty-nine players completed both samples, and no target microRNA differed significantly (p = .07 to .46, small effect sizes), while fatigue scores were unchanged (18.94 to 18.67, p = .684). ICCs were low for four targets and moderate for miR-29c-3p (0.52) and miR-27a-5p (0.65).
paper.limitations: Single team, all male, with no adjustment for sub-concussive impacts, demographics, concussion history or playing position. The authors note that opposing individual changes cancelled out in group means, and Table 1 shows the number of players reporting previous concussions rising from 17 to 20 between collections without saying whether any occurred in-season. Reporting inconsistencies: the methods name miR-30e-5p but the results use miR-30c-5p; the abstract gives an ICC range of -.04 to .65, while Table 2 includes -0.16 for miR-7-1-3p; and the sign of the post-season miR-29c-3p median differs between Table 2 and the text.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not treat a change in these salivary microRNAs as a sign of concussion, because the markers varied between pre-season and post-season samples in a cohort the authors describe as without a diagnosed concussive event. The results do not support using this panel in concussion decisions, as the authors conclude.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not inform training or performance decisions. It did not test salivary microRNA as a load or fatigue marker, so it gives no basis for using it that way.
paper.rtp: Not usable for return-to-sport or concussion clearance decisions. The study did not sample athletes at the time of or after a concussion, and its low reliability means these markers cannot establish recovery or readiness.

records.sourceFile: Substantiating the use of ultrasound tissue characterization in the analysis of tendon structure - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Rabello LM, Dams OC, van den Akker-Scheek I, Zwerver J, O'Neill S. Substantiating the Use of Ultrasound Tissue Characterization in the Analysis of Tendon Structure: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(3):e161-e175.
paper.abstract: The authors reviewed 27 studies to determine how ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) can predict, diagnose and monitor tendon structure and tendinopathy, and to propose a standard scanning and analysis method. UTC was a possible adjunct for diagnosing Achilles tendinopathy and showed promise for monitoring load and treatment, but its predictive value was inconclusive.
paper.tldr: Ultrasound tissue characterization may help show tendon changes in response to load or treatment and can add diagnostic information in Achilles tendinopathy. It has not been shown to predict who will develop tendinopathy, and scanning methods still need to be standardised before results can be compared.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with two reviewers screening in three rounds (titles, abstracts, then full text) and a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Data were extracted on design, participants, scanning method (position, scan direction, window size, area analysed) and whether UTC was used to predict, diagnose or monitor tendons. The review was narrative and descriptive, with no quality assessment or pooled analysis.
paper.findings: Of 27 included studies, 18 examined the Achilles tendon, 5 the patellar tendon and 4 both. Predictive studies gave inconsistent results for Achilles tendinopathy, while a higher percentage of disorganised tissue (echo types III and IV) was linked to patellar tendinopathy in one study. For diagnosis, UTC separated symptomatic from asymptomatic Achilles tendons in some studies (one reported 83% accuracy). For monitoring, several studies showed changes in echo types after loading or treatment, although results varied across studies. Scanning methods differed widely across studies.
paper.limitations: No formal quality assessment and no pooled analysis because the studies were heterogeneous in design, population and method. Most studies focused on mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, and patellar tendon evidence is limited. Few diagnostic studies exist and there is no gold-standard reference for echo types. The search closed in September 2018 and several authors contributed multiple studies. The abstract reports 1972 search hits while the results report 1351.
paper.practicalImplications: Use UTC as an adjunct to clinical assessment and conventional imaging, not as the sole basis for predicting tendinopathy. If UTC is used to track tendon response to load, use the same standardised method each time (position, scan direction, window size 9 or 17, contours no more than 5 mm apart) and compare repeat scans in the same way.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Consider UTC scans to track how Achilles or patellar tendons adapt to a loading block, using the same protocol each time. Do not use echo-type changes alone to decide how much load an athlete can take, since the link to symptoms is unclear.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: UTC may help monitor tendon structure during rehabilitation, but the review found no clear link between echo-type changes and clinical outcome, so it cannot be used alone to decide when an athlete is ready to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Synthetic peptides in doping control - A powerful tool for an analytical challenge.pdf

paper.citation: Gómez-Guerrero NA, González-López NM, Zapata-Velásquez JD, Martínez-Ramírez JA, Rivera-Monroy ZJ, García-Castañeda JE. Synthetic Peptides in Doping Control: A Powerful Tool for an Analytical Challenge. ACS Omega. 2022;7:38193-38206.
paper.abstract: This review summarizes the role of peptides in doping, with emphasis on reference materials, sample pretreatment, instrumentation and method validation for detecting them in biological samples. The authors propose solid-phase peptide synthesis for in-house reference standards and high-resolution LC-MS for detection.
paper.tldr: Peptide doping agents are hard to detect because they are short-lived and resemble natural molecules. Better reference materials, sample preparation and high-resolution LC-MS methods are the main tools the review identifies for detecting them.
paper.methods: A narrative review of the peptides on the WADA prohibited list, the synthesis and characterization of reference materials, sample pretreatment methods (SPE, liquid-liquid extraction, protein precipitation, immunoaffinity and enzymatic digestion), LC and MS platforms, and the validation guidelines used. No systematic search or inclusion criteria are described.
paper.findings: Peptide hormones, growth factors, insulins and vasopressin analogues are listed in WADA sections S2, S4 and S5, and insulins and similar peptides are hard to detect because of short half-lives and similarity to endogenous molecules. LC or reverse-phase SPE purification can yield synthetic peptides above 95% purity, and the authors propose solid-phase peptide synthesis as a route to in-house reference standards. Reversed-phase LC coupled to high-resolution MS (TOF or Orbitrap) is described as the preferred platform, and cited validation studies report limits of detection from about 0.02 to 20 ng/mL depending on peptide and matrix. The authors note that no specific validation guide has been established for peptides and that, unlike other doping agents, peptides lack adequate reference materials.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative and does not state how studies were selected. Its validation examples draw mainly on spiked samples, clinical trials or pharmacokinetic studies; athlete samples were used less often (one cited study used 209 athlete serum samples for IGF-1). The article reports no clinical outcomes or effects on athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can note that many WADA-listed peptides are short-lived and difficult to detect, so detection capability varies by compound and matrix. The review gives no clinical, training or nutrition protocol, and its findings should not be applied to athlete management.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: the review explains why peptide agents such as growth hormone releasing peptides, insulin and erythropoietin appear on the WADA list, but it does not test their performance effects and gives no training guidance.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: the review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: THE RELATIONSHIP OF INFRARED THERMOGRAPHY WITH THE IDENTIFICATION OF CHANGES IN BIOLOGICAL MARKERS AFTER EXERCISE - A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW.pdf

paper.citation: Nobre TL, Rocha LY, Carbone PO, Grassi MCF, de Oliveira Júnior R, Caperuto EC. The Relationship of Infrared Thermography With the Identification of Changes in Biological Markers After Exercise: A Systematic Review. Journal of Bodywork & Movement Therapies. 2025 (in press).
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review asked whether changes in skin temperature measured by infrared thermography match the inflammatory and muscle-damage changes seen after exercise in trained people. Five studies were included, and the authors found few studies linking the method to biomarkers, with weak or inconsistent associations.
paper.tldr: Infrared thermography is used widely in sport, but it has been tested against blood muscle-damage markers in only five small studies, and most found no clear link. Use it as a screening aid alongside clinical examination, not as a substitute for CK or lactate.
paper.methods: A PRISMA systematic review registered in PROSPERO (CRD42022385463), with searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, LILACS, SciELO, SPORTDiscus and Embase in January 2023 and no language or date restriction. Two reviewers screened full texts, and the included studies were experimental trials of trained athletes of both sexes over 18 that measured infrared skin temperature alongside CK or lactate. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2.
paper.findings: Five studies were included, with 81 athletes in total (10 to 21 per study) from rugby, soccer, sprint and distance running. Bandeira et al. (2014, rugby) found no correlation between skin temperature variation and serum CK. Fernandes et al. (2017, soccer) found skin temperature and CK moderately related in all regions after two consecutive matches, with CK higher 48 h after the second match. Korman et al. (2021, sprinters) found no correlation between leg skin temperature and CK over a 10-day camp. Perez-Guarner et al. (2019, half-marathon) reported that a regression model could not predict physiological stress from skin temperature, and Table 2 reports no skin temperature increase after the race. Rojas-Valverde et al. (2021, marathon) found higher skin temperature the day after the race but no correlation with muscle damage markers.
paper.limitations: The authors note the small number of studies, differing protocols and sports, and few time points, which made correlation hard to establish. Most studies were rated uncertain on the reference standard domain of QUADAS-2. The text reports 55 men and 26 women, but Table 1 gives 60 men and 21 women, and the discussion says skin temperature rose 24 h before and 48 h after the half-marathon while Table 2 reports no post-race rise, so the table values are used here. Bandeira et al. measured only 48 h after training or a match, so no pre-session baseline existed.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use infrared thermography to flag skin-temperature asymmetry for clinical follow-up, as the authors suggest, together with clinical examination. On current evidence it should not be used as a stand-in for CK or lactate to judge muscle damage after training or matches. Future protocols should measure skin temperature and biomarkers before and after sessions.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: skin temperature changes were seen after matches, marathons and camps, but they did not consistently track muscle-damage markers. Using it to periodize training load would need baseline measures and a validated link to load, which these studies do not provide.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: no included study examined injury recovery, rehabilitation or return to play, so the review cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its use for injury screening is discussed by the authors but not tested in these studies.

records.sourceFile: Techniques to derive and clean acceleration and deceleration data of athlete tracking technologies in team sports - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Ellens S, Middleton K, Gastin PB, Varley MC. Techniques to derive and clean acceleration and deceleration data of athlete tracking technologies in team sports: A scoping review. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
paper.abstract: This scoping review mapped how acceleration and deceleration data from athlete tracking technologies in team sports are derived, cleaned and applied. A systematic search of four databases identified 276 eligible studies. Most studies (60%) did not report how the data were derived and cleaned, and the data were most often used as effort-based metrics to describe movement demands.
paper.tldr: Acceleration and deceleration metrics from GPS and tracking systems depend heavily on how the raw data were derived, filtered and thresholded. Most published studies do not say what processing they used, so their numbers are hard to compare.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and JBI methodology, with PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science searched from inception to August 2020 using sport, acceleration and tracking-technology terms. After screening 5015 records and assessing 354 full texts, 276 studies were included. Derivation, cleaning and metric criteria were extracted with a custom template.
paper.findings: Most included studies used acceleration measures (n = 270) and 148 used deceleration measures. The derivation technique was not specified in 66% of studies and 88% did not mention any data cleaning; of studies that cleaned data, 48% used a low-pass Butterworth filter with cut-off frequencies from 0.02 to 15 Hz, rarely with a rationale. Number of efforts was the most used metric, and 59% of those studies defined an effort only by a set threshold.
paper.limitations: The review did not assess study quality and included only English-language publications up to August 2020. One author ran the search and title screening, and two authors screened abstracts and full texts. The headline percentages are inconsistent across sections (abstract 60% with no derivation or cleaning information; results 66% derivation unspecified and 88% no cleaning; discussion 92% no cleaning), and the findings apply to team sports only.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should record which device, software version, derivation method, filter and cut-off, and effort criteria were used before comparing acceleration or deceleration counts across studies or systems. Metric thresholds and minimum effort durations should be stated alongside any reported effort counts.
paper.athleteDev: Acceleration and deceleration effort counts depend on the tracking system, derivation method and cleaning filter used. Compare athletes or periods only within the same system and settings, and report those settings with the data.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It maps data processing methods across team-sport studies and contains no injured-athlete outcomes or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Ten word list performance in healthy athletes and athletes at 3 to 5 days following concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Hutchison MG, Di Battista AP, Pyndiura KL, Corallo DN, Lawrence DW, Richards D. Ten-word list performance in healthy athletes and athletes at 3-to-5 days following concussion. Clin J Sport Med. 2021.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of 363 healthy university athletes measured at preseason and 49 university athletes tested a median of 4 days after sport-related concussion, using the 10-word recall task from the SCAT-5. Recall did not differ between groups, and healthy females outperformed healthy males on both immediate and delayed recall.
paper.tldr: The SCAT-5 10-word recall did not separate university athletes about 4 days after concussion from healthy athletes tested at preseason. Females recalled slightly more words than males at baseline, so sex should be considered when interpreting scores.
paper.methods: Healthy university athletes completed preseason baseline testing (n = 363) and athletes with sport-related concussion were tested at a median of 4.0 days after injury (n = 49). Immediate recall (three trials, maximum 30) and delayed recall (one trial, maximum 10) of the 10-word list were compared between groups with separate analyses for males and females. Symptoms were recorded with an expanded 27-item Post-Concussion Symptom Scale.
paper.findings: No significant difference in immediate recall (P = 0.228, Cohen's d = 0.18) or delayed recall (P = 0.908, Cohen's d = 0.02) between concussed and healthy athletes, and the null result held in male and female subsets. In healthy athletes, females scored higher than males on immediate recall (mean difference 1.0, P = 0.002) and delayed recall (mean difference 0.5, P = 0.006).
paper.limitations: The concussed group was small (n = 49) and was compared with healthy athletes measured at a different time, not with its own preinjury baseline. The authors state that a larger concussed sample would have allowed subgroup analyses by sport type and concussion history, and controlling for the number of tests. The concussed athletes were older and more often had a concussion history than the healthy group (results held after adjustment), and the abstract conflicts with the results on the male count (220 vs 210) and the sex-difference P value for immediate recall (P < 0.001 vs P = 0.002); results values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: In the 3 to 5 day window, the SCAT-5 10-word recall test did not separate concussed university athletes from healthy peers in this study. Staff should interpret scores with sex in mind and should not use this test alone to rule concussion in or out.
paper.athleteDev: Use this as a baseline measure of the SCAT-5 10-word recall, noting that females scored higher than males at baseline in this sample. Do not use the 10-word list as a standalone marker of cognitive change.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport. It compared groups at one subacute time point and measured no return-to-play decisions or outcomes, and a normal recall score does not show that concussion has resolved.

records.sourceFile: Test and evaluation of heart rate derived core temperature algorithms for use in NCAA Division I football athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Hagen J, Himmler A, Clark J, Ramadan J, Stone J, Divine J, et al. Test and evaluation of heart rate derived core temperature algorithms for use in NCAA Division I football athletes. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2020;5:46.
paper.abstract: Validation study comparing heart-rate-derived core temperature estimates from Zephyr BioHarness devices with an ingestible core temperature pill in 13 male Division I football athletes during summer training camp. Overall concordance was 0.643, and concordance was 0.834 in the upper body fat group (above 6.0%).
paper.tldr: Heart-rate-derived core temperature agreed only moderately with an ingestible pill in college football players during camp (concordance 0.643, which the authors call poor, with 78% of readings within 1 F). Agreement was much better in athletes above 6% body fat, and readings above about 102.5 F were rarely tested.
paper.methods: Thirteen male Division I football athletes who were full participants in practice wore Zephyr BioHarness devices, which give an estimated core temperature (ECT) from heart rate, and swallowed an ingestible radio-frequency core temperature pill during summer training camp. Athletes were split into upper (above 6.0% body fat, n = 6) and lower (6.0% or below, n = 7) groups. Agreement was assessed with Lin's concordance correlation, Bland-Altman analysis and difference histograms.
paper.findings: Overall concordance was 0.643 and 78% of paired values fell within +/-1.0 F of the pill. Overall bias was -0.192 F (95% CI -0.333 to -0.05), with limits of agreement of -1.803 to 1.42 F. In the upper body fat group, concordance was 0.834, 93% of values were within +/-1.0 F, and the authors report better accuracy than in the lower body fat group.
paper.limitations: The sample was 13 male athletes from one team and one camp, so results may not generalise to other teams, sexes or conditions. The body-fat subgroups were small (6 and 7), so subgroup estimates are imprecise. Only 134 paired measurements were collected, and the post hoc power analysis showed 402 pairs would be needed for the full group, while most pill temperatures stayed below 102.5 F, so accuracy in the clinically important range above 105 F is untested. The 3-h pill ingestion window may not fully remove cold-water interference.
paper.practicalImplications: Heart-rate-derived core temperature may help flag heat strain during football camp, but single readings can underestimate the pill by up to about 2 F. It was not validated at temperatures that signal exertional heat stroke, so it should not replace direct core temperature measurement when heat illness is suspected, and accuracy is lower in leaner athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Use heart-rate-derived core temperature to track relative heat strain across camp sessions for football players, not as an exact core temperature for each athlete. Interpret values with the wide limits of agreement in mind.
paper.rtp: This validation study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It tested no injured athletes and no return-to-play or recovery outcomes, and it does not establish that the device can guide re-entry after exertional heat illness.

records.sourceFile: The ALR‐RSI score can be used to evaluate psychological readiness to return to sport after acute Achilles tendon tear.pdf

paper.citation: Shitrit E, Valentin E, Baudrier N, Bohu Y, Rauline G, Lopes R, et al. The ALR-RSI score can be used to evaluate psychological readiness to return to sport after acute Achilles tendon tear. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2023;31:4961-4968.
paper.abstract: The study validated the ALR-RSI, a psychological readiness to return to sport score, after Achilles tendon repair in 50 patients using COSMIN methods. The score correlated strongly with EFAS, FAAM and VISA-A, discriminated patients who returned to sport from those who did not, and showed excellent reproducibility and internal consistency.
paper.tldr: The French ALR-RSI psychological readiness score appears valid and reproducible after Achilles tendon repair in a small series of 50 patients. It may help flag patients who need psychological support, but it has not been tested for prediction in a new group.
paper.methods: Validation following COSMIN methodology in patients who played sport at least monthly and had open Achilles repair at three centres. Patients completed the ALR-RSI, VISA-A, EFAS and FAAM 6 to 9 months after surgery, and 10 patients repeated the ALR-RSI after 15 days.
paper.findings: 11 of 50 patients (22%) had returned to sport at a mean follow-up of 6.8 months, 4 at their pre-injury level and 7 at a lower level. ALR-RSI correlated strongly with EFAS (r = 0.68), FAAM Sport (r = 0.70), FAAM AVQ (r = 0.60) and VISA-A (r = 0.54). Scores were lower in non-returners (60.7 vs 83.2, p = 0.001), with an AUC of 0.83; a cut-off of 77.5 gave 82% sensitivity and 79% specificity, and none of the AUCs differed significantly between scores. Test-retest ICC was 0.99 in 10 patients and Cronbach alpha was 0.95. Sport type and level were not associated with return to sport.
paper.limitations: The sample is small, with only 11 returners, and the authors note that a 12-month follow-up could have improved discrimination. The study only covered open repairs, and the null association of sport type and level with return to sport may reflect low power, as the authors note. The reproducibility sample is 10 patients.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians could use the ALR-RSI alongside physical scores during Achilles repair rehabilitation to track psychological readiness and identify patients who may need psychological support. The 77.5 cut-off needs confirmation in an independent group before it is used to make return decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measures no performance outcomes after return. Its use for performance staff is limited to a psychological readiness check during rehabilitation.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The score can track psychological readiness to return to sport 6 to 9 months after Achilles repair. It cannot show when an athlete is physically ready, cannot predict who will return, and was validated against questionnaires rather than objective return criteria.

records.sourceFile: The Concurrent Validity of Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion Workload Obtained Face-to-Face Versus Via an Online ApplicationA Team Case S.pdf

paper.citation: Fox JL, O'Grady CJ, Scanlan AT. The Concurrent Validity of Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion Workload Obtained Face-to-Face Versus Via an Online Application: A Team Case Study. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors compared session RPE collected face-to-face in one season with session RPE collected by a phone-based online app in another season, in 16 semiprofessional male basketball players. Face-to-face ratings correlated more strongly with PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zone workload than the app ratings did.
paper.tldr: In this one team, session RPE collected face-to-face tracked objective workload more closely than session RPE collected through a phone app. Basketball staff should check any app-based RPE against objective load before relying on it.
paper.methods: Observational team case study across the 2018 and 2019 seasons. Players rated session RPE after each session, either face-to-face (2018) or through a phone-based app (2019), and workload was measured by microsensor PlayerLoad and summated heart rate zones. Repeated-measures correlations with 95% confidence intervals were used to compare the two reporting methods.
paper.findings: All correlations were significant. Face-to-face session RPE correlated large with PlayerLoad (r = .69) and very large with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .74). The online app correlated small with PlayerLoad (r = .29) and moderate with summated heart rate zone workload (r = .34).
paper.limitations: The two methods were compared in different seasons with partly different players, so season and method cannot be separated. Ratings were collected within 30 minutes (face-to-face) and within 60 minutes (online), heart rate was measured with different devices each season, and lower compliance with the app left 57 samples against 163 face-to-face.
paper.practicalImplications: Collect session RPE face-to-face or within a short, consistent window, and do not assume app-based RPE has the same validity. Check any app-based RPE against objective workload before using it to guide training.
paper.athleteDev: For basketball training load monitoring, the results favour collecting session RPE individually and soon after training. App-based RPE should be checked against PlayerLoad or heart rate zone workload before it guides load decisions.
paper.rtp: The study is about training load monitoring in healthy players and does not address injury or return to sport. It cannot be used to set return-to-play loads.

records.sourceFile: The Functional Movement Screen’s Ability to Detect Changes in Movement Patterns After a Training Intervention.pdf

paper.citation: Minthorn LM, Fayson SD, Stobierski LM, Welch CE, Anderson BE. The Functional Movement Screen’s Ability to Detect Changes in Movement Patterns After a Training Intervention. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2015;24(3):322-326.
paper.abstract: Clinical question: does an individualised training programme improve movement patterns in adults who participate in high-intensity activities? The authors searched for level 3 or higher studies that used the Functional Movement Screen (FMS) before and after a training programme. Three studies met the criteria. One study found no significant change after a 12-week programme, and two reported significant changes in movement patterns. The clinical bottom line is inconsistent evidence (grade C).
paper.tldr: Evidence that individualised training improves Functional Movement Screen patterns is inconsistent: two of three studies found gains and one found none. Use the FMS alongside other outcome measures, and do not read a higher FMS score as proof of better performance or lower injury risk.
paper.methods: Critically appraised topic. Searches of the Cochrane Library, Medline, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus, plus reference lists and hand search, covered 2004 to 2013 and English-language studies. Eligible studies were level 3 or higher, used the FMS before and after an individualised training programme in physically active individuals or athletes, and excluded people under 18, those with current musculoskeletal injury, and those with restricted training. The three studies were graded by Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels.
paper.findings: Bodden et al (cluster randomised trial, level 1b, mixed martial arts athletes) and Kiesel et al (cohort, level 2b, professional football players) reported significant changes in movement patterns after training. Frost et al (single-blinded randomised trial, level 1b) reported no significant change after a 12-week programme. Baseline FMS scores were similar across groups (12.8 to 13.3), except football linemen (11.8). The Frost programme targeted whole-body coordination and fitness rather than specific movement limitations.
paper.limitations: Only three studies were appraised, and their designs and programmes differ. Kiesel et al had no control group, so gains could not be separated from repeated testing. The authors note that FMS gains may reflect participants' knowledge of the grading criteria, and that little evidence links higher FMS scores to better athletic performance. The Implications section attributes the non-significant result to study 3 (Kiesel), while the Results and Discussion attribute it to study 2 (Frost); the Results and Discussion are followed here.
paper.practicalImplications: Exercises that directly address the movement patterns the FMS identifies may improve scores, whereas whole-body coordination or general fitness programmes may not. Use the FMS as one component of a wider assessment, and add other outcome measures when judging whether a training programme is working.
paper.athleteDev: When an athlete's FMS shows a specific movement limitation, a corrective programme aimed at that pattern may improve the score, while a general fitness block is less likely to. Judge the programme by more than the FMS score, because score gains have not been shown to carry over to athletic performance.
paper.rtp: It cannot guide return to sport or clearance. The included studies tested participants without current injury, and the authors state that it is unknown whether resolving movement limitations reduces injury risk.
